solution_full: Coefficient determinant: $\Delta=1(10-3p)-1(5-p)+1(3-2)=6-2p$. The system has a unique solution exactly when $p\ne3$; for $p=3$ it has either none or infinitely many, so these pairs are excluded.
So $z=\dfrac{q-5}{6-2p}$, and $z$ is an integer exactly when $6-2p$ divides $q-5$, where $q-5$ ranges over $-4,-3,\dots,5$.
$p=2$ or $p=4$: $6-2p=\pm2$; the even values of $q-5$ are $-4,-2,0,2,4$, giving $5$ pairs each, $10$ in all.
$p=1$ or $p=5$: $6-2p=\pm4$; the multiples of $4$ are $-4,0,4$, giving $3$ pairs each, $6$ in all.
Total $=10+6+5=21$. Forgetting the pairs with $z=0$ gives $12$; counting all unique-solution pairs gives $90$.
originality_note: New: counting parameter pairs for which the Cramer quotient z = (q-5)/(6-2p) is an integer, combining the uniqueness condition with a divisibility count (way 5). Closest known: classifying a system as unique / none / infinite for given p, q. Different because: the classification is only the filter; the count needs the explicit Cramer value of one unknown.

concept_use.Cramer's rule: z = Delta_3/Delta = (q-5)/(6-2p) by Cramer's rule, which turns the integrality condition into a divisibility count.
concept_use.System of linear equations: The system has a unique solution exactly when the coefficient determinant 6-2p is non-zero, which removes p = 3.

stem_review: Read as a student: p, q integers in 1..10; 'unique solution in which z is an integer' has one reading; ordered pairs. Checked by brute force over all 100 pairs: 90 unique, 21 with integer z. Answer 21 at (D) as planned. Changed: No change.
key_step: Cramer gives z = (q-5)/(6-2p); count divisibility cases with p != 3.
justification: Two short determinants and a small case count; routine, but the count has a trap (z = 0). Comparable to 2024-P1-Q14 (L2), a counting question on matrices with options.
